claims.text: Introducing approximately 1 wt% oxygen into a BCC HfNbTaTiZr-type refractory high-entropy alloy causes coherent nanoscale oxide precipitates to form in situ.
The precipitates formed by oxygen introduction include HfO2 or TiO2.
The oxide precipitates are distributed within grains and along grain boundaries.
The oxide precipitates produce local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions associated with the oxide precipitates act as dislocation-pinning centers.
Dislocation pinning by the oxide precipitates increases yield strength at intermediate temperatures.
The oxide precipitates modify local bond stiffness.
The oxide precipitates upshift phonon-scattering frequencies.
Precipitate-induced changes in bond stiffness and phonon scattering reduce the rate at which elastic modulus decreases with temperature.
The oxygen-enhanced alloy will have more than 10% greater yield strength than the oxygen-lean baseline between approximately 300 and 800 K.
The oxygen-enhanced alloy will have a higher low-temperature elastic modulus than the oxygen-lean baseline.
The oxygen-enhanced alloy will show less temperature dependence of elastic modulus than the oxygen-lean baseline over 300–1200 K.
TEM will reveal a significantly higher density of uniformly distributed coherent oxide precipitates in the oxygen-enhanced alloy.
Processing the baseline alloy in an inert atmosphere with less than 0.01 wt% oxygen results in negligible oxide-precipitate formation.
The proposed comparison holds alloy identity, strain rate, and loading conditions constant while varying oxygen exposure.
A representative oxygen-introduction treatment is 1100 °C for 2 hours under controlled oxygen partial pressure.
The proposed mechanism is bounded to BCC refractory high-entropy alloys containing near 1 wt% oxygen and tested over 300–1200 K.
The effect may be alloy-specific and may differ in non-BCC high-entropy alloys.
